Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette:
Elena had always trusted her training. Twenty-nine years on the force, the last twelve as a detective, and she had learned to read a scene the way other people read a book. So when the call came in about the illegal chemical dump in the industrial district, she did what she always did: she walked in first, without waiting for HAZMAT. The warehouse was dim, the air thick with something sweet and chemical, like artificial fruit left to rot. She remembered thinking it smelled like a hospital’s basement, that clean-sterile-underneath-a-rotten-sweetness that made her wrinkle her nose. She had taken two deep breaths before her partner yelled at her to get out. That was two years ago. Now, every time she feels short of breath—walking up stairs, carrying groceries, even just lying in bed at night—she is back in that warehouse. The memory does not come as a story with a beginning and an end. It comes in pieces: the sting in her sinuses, the yellow haze of the light, the sound of her own footsteps echoing on concrete. She tries to hold onto the whole picture, but before she can, she pushes it away. It feels like she is still standing there, her lungs burning, the smell of antiseptic and sweat filling her nose, and she has to cover her face with her hands to make it stop.

The department cleared her medically after six months. Her lung function tests came back normal. But Elena does not feel normal. She has come to believe that something inside her is permanently broken, that she will never feel ordinary emotions again—no joy, no calm, just a constant low hum of readiness. Her body stays tense, as if bracing for a blow that never lands. She scans every room she enters: the corners, the exits, the faces of strangers. When a car backfires or a door slams, she flinches so hard that her coffee splashes onto her desk. She cannot stop herself from being on high alert, and she has decided that this is just how she has to live now. She has to be on guard all the time, because no one else is going to protect her.

The betrayal feels worse than the exposure. She had trusted the department to have her back, to have protocols in place. Instead, she walked into a toxic cloud because the call had been misrouted and the HAZMAT team was twenty minutes late. The people who should have kept her safe had let her down, and now she cannot be around authority figures without her stomach knotting. She avoids her lieutenant. She takes the stairs to avoid passing the uniformed officers in the hallway. She has started working cases from her laptop at home, claiming she needs quiet for paperwork, but the truth is that the sight of a badge or a duty belt makes her want to run.

Her ex-husband called last week, asking if she wanted to meet for coffee. She said she was busy. She was not busy. She was sitting on her couch, watching the door, her hands pressed over her nose and mouth. When she cannot escape a triggering smell or a sudden sound, she forces her mind elsewhere—she thinks of grocery lists, of old movie plots, of anything except the warehouse. But the redirection never lasts. The fragmented pieces always come back.

She finally called the department’s employee assistance program after a night shift when a janitor mopped the floor with bleach, and she spent forty minutes locked in the bathroom, gasping, convinced she was dying. The intake worker asked what she hoped to get from therapy. Elena said she wanted to stop being afraid of her own body. She did not say that what she really fears is that the woman who walked into that warehouse without hesitation is gone, and she does not know how to get her back.
